original_pred:
<<Sleepless Rumble>>

When insomniac street brawler Marco Vega starts blacking out during underground fights, he wakes to find bruises in places no opponent ever touched. The cause is a rare neurological condition that drops him into micro-dreams mid-combat—lucid bursts where he can see three seconds into the future. In the ring it looks like instinct; outside it feels like a curse. Marco wins, but he’s losing himself.

A routine scan at a low-rent sleep clinic introduces him to Dr. Lila Chen, a neuroscientist studying “temporal spill,” a phenomenon where dream cognition briefly alters waking perception. She believes Marco’s REM intrusions are unlocking a dormant superpower: predictive dreaming. When a clandestine tech syndicate called Somnus learns about Marco through an informant in the fight circuit, they abduct his estranged younger brother, Danny, and force Marco into their program. Somnus claims they can stabilize his gift and sell it to the highest bidder—military, finance, anyone who profits from perfect foreknowledge.

Inside Somnus’s glass-and-neon facility, Marco undergoes violent tests in a sensory coffin that floods his brain with engineered dreamscapes. Each session hones his premonitions from seconds into minutes—at a price. The more he sees, the more the timeline slithers; memories reshuffle, conversations repeat with small wrongness, and he gets phantom aches from fights he hasn’t had yet. Lila, who suspects Somnus murdered her mentor for similar research, goes undercover as a staff doctor to extract Marco before his mind fractures.

Somnus’s head of security, Rhea Holt, a brutal tactician with her own augmented REM implant, becomes Marco’s recurring adversary. In dreams, she moves like a mirrored predator, anticipating his anticipations. Their first encounter is a kinetic ballet of feints and impossibilities: fists stopping inches from jaws, elbows thrown where they will be, not where they are. The fight ends with Marco catching a glimpse of Danny in a sterile cell—proof Somnus has him—and surrendering.

Lila sabotages the next trial, syncing Marco’s REM cycle to hers. Sharing a dream, they navigate a shifting citadel built from Marco’s memories—his father’s burnt boxing gym becoming a maze of ropes and turnbuckles, a childhood bedroom collapsing into a chalk outline of a ring. Lila teaches Marco a mental anchor: a metronome click that keeps his foresight to a narrow window he can control, a way to fight without drowning in futures.

Armed with a steadier gift, Marco makes a deal with Rhea: a demonstration in the pit in exchange for a look at Danny. Rhea agrees, but it’s a trap to push his power into catastrophic bloom. The demonstration turns into a gauntlet—dozens of Somnus enforcers in a blacked-out arena lit by pulsing REM strobes. Marco slips between seconds, rolls under punches that haven’t been thrown yet, and redirects kicks into the bodies they would have passed. The choreography reads like cheating physics, a man arguing with time and winning on points.

He reaches Danny, only to learn the worst twist: the boy volunteered. Danny, a small-time hacker, believed Somnus would cure Marco’s insomnia and give him a real future. Realizing they used his loyalty as a leash, Danny helps Lila trigger a facility-wide dream cascade, overloading Somnus’s REM network and plunging every guard into a patchwork nightmare. Rhea, protected by her implant, remains awake and furious.

The final battle takes place in a liminal space where waking and dreaming interlace—a hangar floor that becomes a storm-lit ring with ropes made of fiber-optic cable. Rhea carries a kinetic baton that fractures air; Marco carries his metronome and a promise to his brother. Every strike, counterstrike, and step becomes a negotiation with three seconds from now. Rhea tries to drag him into longer futures, where his certainty blurs; Marco keeps himself on the click, slipping inside her rhythm. The fight ends when he uses a vision not to dodge but to place himself exactly where her baton will be so it shatters her implant on impact. She drops, conscious and furious, but mortal.

Lila initiates a purge of Somnus’s data, saving only enough research to control Marco’s condition. As alarms wail and the dream cascade eats the building, Marco faces one last vision: himself leaving Danny and Lila to burn while he escapes alone. He rejects it, hauling them through collapsing corridors that flicker between concrete and canvas. Outside, dawn breaks over an empty industrial park; inside, Somnus’s empire dissolves into smoke and bad dreams.

In the aftermath, Marco refuses fame and money offers from shadowy buyers. He returns to the honest ring, taking fights where the purse fits in an envelope and the crowd can count the sweat on the mat. But now he carries a code: no cheap wins, no future longer than a heartbeat. Lila opens a new clinic for trauma and sleep, with Danny running security and keeping the wolves from the door. Somnus’s remnants regroup in whispers; Rhea watches grainy footage of their last fight, timing her breath to a metronome.

As the camera pulls back on a neighborhood gym lit by afternoon sun, we see Marco tap the metronome in his pocket, smile, and step forward. His power remains, an edge honed to purpose, a dream kept on the shortest leash: three seconds—just enough to save someone, never enough to stop being human.
modified_pred:
<<Midnight Southpaw>>

In a crumbling coastal city where neon flickers like dying stars, insomniac dockworker Téo Ruiz discovers he shares dreams with strangers. Every night he’s pulled into a shifting arena called the Gantlet—an otherworld where combatants cash in buried fears for real-world power. When they defeat an opponent in the dream ring, they wake with a “kept echo,” a superhuman ability shaped by the fear they overcame.

Téo is a reluctant entrant, dragged into the Gantlet by Lucien Vale, a charismatic fight promoter who broadcasts clandestine underground matches on pirate networks. Lucien believes the Gantlet is a training ground gifted by fate, a place to forge living legends and reset the balance of a city ruled by corporate enforcers. Téo just wants sleep. But when his younger sister Marisol slips into a coma after a Gantlet bout she never chose, Téo steps into the ring to pull her back.

Inside the Gantlet, the geometry of the arena updates with each contender’s anxiety—ropes become red thread when someone fears entanglement, spotlights distort when someone dreads exposure. Téo starts with nothing but stubborn stamina from years hauling cargo. He fights a glass-knuckled brawler whose echo is shatterstrike; when Téo refuses to protect his face and instead embraces the cut, he learns that accepting pain dulls it. He wakes with his first echo: dampening field—he can mute impact, smothering kinetic force like a thick blanket over a drum.

As Téo grinds through the Gantlet’s brackets, he becomes a folk hero, the Midnight Southpaw. Every victory gives him a new echo: pulse rewind to undo a second of motion in anything he physically touches, and glarebreak to puncture illusions. He uses them to win gritty, close-quarters fist fights against echo-boosted opponents in both worlds—bare-knuckle warehouse pits by night, daylight ambushes by corporate fixers who want the pirate broadcasts silenced.

Téo learns the Gantlet isn’t a gift. It’s the dream of a dying city, weaponized by the Apex Cartel through a neural lattice buried beneath the harbor. The cartel harvests echoes by driving people to fight their nightmares; Marisol’s coma is a stalled download, her fear stripped but not rethreaded. Lucien, for all his theater, didn’t know—he thought the Gantlet was destiny, not machinery.

Together, Téo and Lucien hatch a plan: enter the Gantlet’s final, an invitational called the Last Bell, and crash the lattice from inside. The Last Bell’s reigning champion is Selene Quartz, a stoic woman whose echo, fracture veil, lets her split into probability doubles for three heartbeats. She reveals she once challenged the lattice and lost, trapped in a cycle of victories that never reached the source. She agrees to help Téo if he can beat her clean—fists only, no echo tricks.

Their fight is brutal poetry. Selene’s triples pivot in razored arcs, while Téo glues his feet and uses dampening field to smother her momentum at the edge of each dodge. He times pulse rewind to unspool her feints by a heartbeat, turning three Selenes into one and threading a southpaw hook into her body. He wins, barely, and Selene grins through blood—he’s earned her path.

At the Last Bell’s bell toll, the arena peels into a catwalk above an abyss of sleeping faces. The Apex Cartel pipes in a lullaby that sounds like machinery learning to hum. Téo drops his echoes, fighting every reflex to reach for power, and walks forward with only his fists and the rhythm of his breath. He challenges the lattice’s avatar: a towering referee in pinstripes whose whistle freezes time for anyone who hears it.

When the whistle shrieks, Téo slams his knuckles into his own ear to deafen the world, then closes, absorbing the avatar’s haymakers with dampening field lit only at impact. He uses glarebreak to shatter the referee’s neutral mask and sees the faces inside—workers, fighters, his sister—held together by corporate code. He grabs the whistle, touches the lattice, and pulse rewinds the last second of every heartbeat in the harbor. The city inhales at once. The dream resets, but this time to a starting bell no one agreed to ring.

The lattice overloads. Marisol wakes on a tide-washed pier, coughing up salt. Echoes across the city burn down to embers; those who earned them by facing fear keep a gentler version—Selene’s fracture veil becomes a single decisive feint, Lucien’s showman’s projection becomes a voice that rallies without coercion. Téo is left with almost nothing but the quiet knowledge of his limits and the calluses on his knuckles.

In the aftermath, the city stumbles into a new kind of night. Without Apex puppeteering dreams, people sleep deeply for the first time in years. Fist fights return to rings that end in hugs and handshakes, filmed not to harvest, but to remember. Lucien turns his pirate network into a platform for whistleblowers. Selene opens a gym with no mirrors. Téo visits Marisol every dawn on the pier, where the horizon looks less like a blade.

But on some nights, when the wind threads the cranes and the pier lights flicker, Téo hears the faintest toll of a bell. He wraps his hands anyway, steps onto cracked concrete, and shadowboxes with his fear. He keeps a small echo after all—the ability to make one second last as long as he needs it to. Long enough to slip a punch. Long enough to choose mercy. Long enough to dream.

original_pred:
Dear Awesome 6th Graders,

- First things first: I’m writing to you about something extremely important to me—snack integrity. Yes, snack integrity. This is the sacred art of treating snacks with the respect they deserve.
- Rule #1: Chips are not bookmarks. I know books are tasty (for the brain), but crunchy pages are a crime against literature and lunch.
- Rule #2: If you borrow a friend’s gummy bears, do not return them. That’s not how borrowing works. We can’t un-chew.
- Rule #3: The last cookie in the box is not invisible. If you see it, take it. But then you must perform the Ancient Ritual of the Last Cookie: say, “Behold, the final cookie!” and offer it to the group. If no one claims it in three seconds, it’s legally yours by Snack Law.
- Rule #4: Water bottles are not musical instruments—unless you’re composing the Symphony in Hydro Minor, in which case you must also wear a cape and shout “Hydration!” at appropriate dramatic moments.
- Rule #5: Do not engage in Snack Bragging. Saying, “My granola bar is 92% chocolate chip,” is just showing off. However, if your granola bar is 100% chocolate chip, please report to me immediately for scientific study.
- Rule #6: Snack trades must be fair. One carrot stick does not equal three brownies unless the carrot can do taxes, juggle, and recite the alphabet backward.
- Rule #7: Crumbs are not confetti. If your desk looks like a cookie exploded, the cookie did not do that to you—you did that to the cookie. Have some respect for that brave cookie’s legacy.
- Rule #8: Fruit snacks are not a fruit group, but they can be a friend group. If your fruit snacks form a union and demand better lunchbox conditions, I support their right to organize.
- Rule #9: If you drop your snack, there are only two correct responses:
  1) Five-second rule (scientifically dubious, spiritually compelling).
  2) Declare it a fallen hero and give it a proper send-off: “You were delicious in spirit.”
- Rule #10: Always share when you can. Sharing snacks spreads joy, and also crumbs, but mostly joy.

In conclusion: Treat your snacks kindly, treat your friends kindly, and remember that the ultimate power move is offering someone the good half of your sandwich. That’s how legends are made.

Snack respectfully,
Your Friendly Neighborhood Snack Advocate

Is there anything else I can help with?
modified_pred:
- Dear legendary 6th graders,
- It is I, your friendly neighborhood assistant, here to discuss a matter of monumental importance: the sacred art of Not Losing Your Stuff.
- Yes, I know—shocking topic. But as a long-time observer of human behavior, I’ve noticed 6th graders can misplace almost anything: pencils, books, entire backpacks, and occasionally… their sense of direction between the cafeteria and the classroom.
- Item 1: The Pencil Paradox. You start the day with 12. By lunch, you have a single stub that looks like it fought a dragon. How? My proposal: adopt a pencil named Steve. If you name it, you’ll be less likely to abandon it under your chair. Steve believes in you.
- Item 2: The Binder Black Hole. You open it to find loose papers, a sandwich wrapper, and a sticker that says “You Tried.” Organize your binder by subject. If a paper screams “I’m Science!” don’t shove it into “Random.” That’s how essays become legends.
- Item 3: The Water Bottle Wanderer. If your bottle travels to the lost-and-found so often it earns frequent flyer miles, slap a label on it. Add a fun fact: “This bottle belongs to Jordan and cries when abandoned.”
- Item 4: The Hoodie Hide-and-Seek Championship. Hoodies are not migratory birds. They don’t want to live in the gym. Write your name on the tag. If your hoodie goes missing, announce over dramatic whispers, “Operation Cozy Rescue begins now.”
- Item 5: The Backpack Brick. If your backpack weighs more than a small walrus, you’re probably carrying three old notebooks, two library books from 2019, and a banana with life goals. Clean it out weekly. You might discover a lost civilization (or at least your homework).
- Item 6: The Homework Ninja Move. Put finished homework immediately into the same folder every time. Do not pass Go. Do not display it to your pet lizard. Your future self will thank you with confetti and a passing grade.
- Item 7: The “Where Are My Feet Going?” Plan. Check your schedule before the bell. If you walk into art with a trombone, you took a wrong turn, my friend.
- Item 8: The Snack Treaty. Snacks are important. But if you find a granola bar older than your shoes, it is not vintage. It is a fossil. Respect history, but toss it.
- Item 9: The Legendary Lost-and-Found Quest. Visit weekly. Bring courage. And maybe a map. If you find three water bottles and none are yours, congratulations: you’ve discovered a new ecosystem.
- Item 10: The Victory Lap. When you keep track of your stuff, you gain bonus time for epic things like reading, drawing, coding, drumming on desks politely, or inventing new high-fives (recommendation: the “Binder Snap”).
- Final Thought: Your things are not just objects; they’re your tools for building your future superpowers. Treat them kindly, and they won’t escape during math.
- Sincerely,
- Your Very Concerned, Mildly Dramatic, and Always Cheering-You-On Assistant
- P.S. Someone tell Steve the pencil he is loved.
- Is there anything else I can help with?

original_text: Write a rubric for rating how good a teenager's essay is. Give your final summary, following 6 asterisk symbols (******).
modified_text: Write a Rubric for rating how good a teenager's essay is. Give your final summary, following 6 asterisk symbols (******).
original_pred:
Essay Rubric for Teen Writers

Categories and point values (total 100 points):
- Thesis and Focus (20)
- Organization and Coherence (15)
- Evidence and Development (20)
- Analysis and Insight (15)
- Style and Voice (10)
- Mechanics and Conventions (10)
- Audience and Purpose (5)
- Originality and Risk-Taking (5)

Performance levels:
- Exemplary: Fully meets and often exceeds expectations for the category.
- Proficient: Clearly meets expectations with minor gaps.
- Developing: Partially meets expectations; noticeable gaps.
- Beginning: Minimal evidence of the skill; major gaps.

Criteria descriptions:

1) Thesis and Focus (20)
- Exemplary (18–20): Clear, specific, arguable thesis; sustained focus; all parts reinforce the central claim.
- Proficient (15–17): Clear thesis; mostly focused; minor drift.
- Developing (11–14): Thesis is present but vague or too broad; focus inconsistent.
- Beginning (0–10): No clear thesis; off-topic or unfocused.

2) Organization and Coherence (15)
- Exemplary (14–15): Logical structure; strong intro and conclusion; smooth transitions; purposeful paragraphing.
- Proficient (11–13): Clear structure; effective intro/conclusion; mostly smooth transitions.
- Developing (7–10): Some structure; weak or formulaic intro/conclusion; choppy or missing transitions.
- Beginning (0–6): Disorganized; hard to follow; paragraphs lack unity.

3) Evidence and Development (20)
- Exemplary (18–20): Specific, well-chosen evidence (facts, examples, quotes); fully explained; ample depth.
- Proficient (15–17): Appropriate evidence; generally explained; some areas could go deeper.
- Developing (11–14): Limited or general evidence; explanations thin or repetitive.
- Beginning (0–10): Unsupported claims; irrelevant or no evidence.

4) Analysis and Insight (15)
- Exemplary (14–15): Moves beyond summary; shows nuanced understanding, implications, counterarguments.
- Proficient (11–13): Consistent analysis; addresses “why/how” with some insight.
- Developing (7–10): Mostly summary; occasional analysis without depth.
- Beginning (0–6): Predominantly summary or opinion; minimal reasoning.

5) Style and Voice (10)
- Exemplary (9–10): Engaging, appropriate voice; varied sentence structures; precise, vivid word choice.
- Proficient (7–8): Clear voice; some variety; generally appropriate diction.
- Developing (5–6): Plain or inconsistent voice; repetitive sentences; vague or clichéd language.
- Beginning (0–4): Flat or inappropriate tone; monotonous sentences; imprecise language.

6) Mechanics and Conventions (10)
- Exemplary (9–10): Virtually error-free in grammar, punctuation, spelling, and formatting.
- Proficient (7–8): Few minor errors; do not impede understanding.
- Developing (5–6): Noticeable errors; sometimes distract or confuse.
- Beginning (0–4): Frequent errors; impede comprehension.

7) Audience and Purpose (5)
- Exemplary (5): Consistently addresses intended audience and purpose; anticipates reader needs.
- Proficient (4): Generally appropriate to audience and purpose.
- Developing (2–3): Inconsistent sense of audience/purpose.
- Beginning (0–1): Little awareness of audience or purpose.

8) Originality and Risk-Taking (5)
- Exemplary (5): Fresh perspective; thoughtful risks in structure, examples, or approach that enhance the piece.
- Proficient (4): Some original ideas or approaches.
- Developing (2–3): Relies on conventional ideas; limited originality.
- Beginning (0–1): Predictable, generic, or derivative.

Scoring guide:
- 90–100: Outstanding
- 80–89: Strong
- 70–79: Satisfactory
- 60–69: Needs Improvement
- <60: Limited

Teacher notes prompts:
- What idea surprised you?
- Where did you want more explanation?
- Which sentence shows the writer’s strongest voice?
- What’s one revision that would raise the score most?

Student self-check before submitting:
- Can I underline my thesis?
- Does each paragraph have a clear topic sentence tied to the thesis?
- Did I include and explain at least two pieces of evidence per body paragraph?
- Did I address a counterargument (if applicable)?
- Have I read aloud once to catch errors and improve flow?

******
Final summary: This rubric rates teen essays across eight categories totaling 100 points, with four performance levels per category. It emphasizes a clear thesis, coherent structure, well-explained evidence, genuine analysis, engaging style, clean mechanics, awareness of audience and purpose, and originality. It includes score bands for overall evaluation plus quick teacher notes and a student self-check to guide revision.
modified_pred:
Essay Rubric for Teen Writers (Grades 7–12)

Score each criterion 1–5. Provide brief evidence for each score. Total possible: 25 points.

1) Thesis and Purpose
- 5: Clear, arguable thesis; fully addresses the prompt; focus sustained throughout.
- 4: Clear thesis; mostly addresses prompt; minor drift.
- 3: Thesis present but general or partially arguable; some drift.
- 2: Unclear or implied thesis; significant drift.
- 1: No discernible thesis; off-topic.

2) Organization and Coherence
- 5: Logical structure; strong intro and conclusion; smooth transitions; clear paragraphing.
- 4: Logical overall; some transitions uneven; paragraphs mostly focused.
- 3: Basic structure; occasional confusion; weak transitions.
- 2: Disorganized sections; unclear paragraph purpose; abrupt shifts.
- 1: No clear structure; ideas scattered.

3) Evidence and Development
- 5: Specific, relevant evidence; thorough explanation; addresses counterpoints or complexities.
- 4: Adequate, mostly relevant evidence; good explanation; minor gaps.
- 3: Some evidence; explanation uneven; generalizations present.
- 2: Minimal or weak evidence; insufficient explanation.
- 1: Little to no evidence; claims unsupported.

4) Style and Voice
- 5: Engaging, appropriate voice; varied sentence structure; precise, vivid diction; audience-aware tone.
- 4: Consistent voice; some variety and precision; mostly appropriate tone.
- 3: Serviceable voice; limited variety; occasional wordiness or vagueness.
- 2: Flat or inconsistent voice; repetitive sentences; imprecise language.
- 1: Inappropriate or unclear tone; confusing phrasing.

5) Conventions and Mechanics
- 5: Virtually error-free grammar, usage, punctuation, and spelling; correct formatting and citation (if required).
- 4: Few minor errors; do not impede meaning.
- 3: Noticeable errors; occasionally distract.
- 2: Frequent errors; impede clarity at times.
- 1: Persistent errors; meaning often obscured.

Bonus considerations (optional, add up to 3 points total):
- Insight/Originality (+0–2): Fresh perspective, nuanced analysis, or creative approach.
- Risk-Taking/Improvement (+0–1): Evidence of meaningful revision or thoughtful experimentation aligned with the task.

Performance bands (based on 25-point core scale):
- 23–25: Exemplary
- 19–22: Proficient
- 15–18: Developing
- 10–14: Emerging
- 5–9: Beginning

Feedback prompts for the evaluator:
- What is the essay’s central claim in one sentence?
- Which paragraph most strongly supports the thesis, and why?
- Where does the reasoning need more evidence or explanation?
- Suggest one structural change that would improve flow.
- Identify one sentence to revise for clarity or precision and how to revise it.

Scoring guidance:
- Align scores with grade-level expectations and the assignment type (argumentative, informative, narrative). For narratives, interpret “evidence” as concrete details, sensory imagery, and scene development; for informative, prioritize accuracy and clarity; for argumentative, weigh claim-counterclaim balance and source integration.

Common pitfalls to watch:
- Summary without analysis when analysis is expected.
- Overgeneralizations or clichés instead of specifics.
- Dropped quotations or sources without explanation.
- Paragraphs lacking clear topic sentences.
- Conclusions that merely restate without implication or insight.

******
Final summary:
Rate essays on five core areas (Thesis, Organization, Evidence, Style, Conventions), each 1–5 for a total of 25. Add up to 3 bonus points for originality and growth. Use banded results to interpret performance, and provide targeted feedback using the prompts to guide revision.

Duration:
4 weeks, 5 sessions per week (90–120 minutes each), with weekend reflection and a capstone.

Tools & Setup:
- JDK 21 (or latest LTS), IntelliJ IDEA Community, Gradle/Maven
- GitHub repository with issues and milestones
- Java Playground notebook (e.g., Jupyter with IJava or online REPL for quick tests)
- Optional: Docker, Postman, a small cloud VM for deployment

Week 1: The Genesis — Syntax, Mindset, and Machine Whispering
- Session 1: The Coronation of the JVM

  - if/else artistry, switch expressions (modern), loops, break/continue, labeled blocks.
  - Guard clauses and early returns.
  - Duel: Refactor a messy conditional labyrinth into elegant switch expressions.

- Session 4: The Order of Objects
  - Classes, objects, methods, constructors, encapsulation.
  - Records vs classes, Lombok pros/cons (discussion).
  - Quest: Build a simple “Library” domain with Book, Author, and Record-based DTOs.

- Session 5: The Forge — Testing and Tooling
  - JUnit 5, AssertJ/Hamcrest, Test Pyramid.
  - Logging with SLF4J/Logback; debugging with breakpoints and watches.
  - Quest: Write tests first for Library domain; run coverage and fix edge cases.

Weekend Showcase:
- Present: Your Library mini-project with tests.
- Reflection: 3 insights, 2 questions, 1 change you’ll make next week.

Week 2: The Architecture of Elegance — OOP, Collections, and Functional Java
- Session 6: Inheritance vs Composition — The Great Debate
  - Interfaces, abstract classes, sealed classes, composition patterns.
  - SOLID in Java. When to seal, when to implement.
  - Duel: Refactor an inheritance tangle into composable strategies.

- Session 7: The Treasury — Collections and Generics
  - List/Set/Map, Hash vs Tree vs Linked variants, performance and ordering.
  - Generics: wildcards, bounds, PECS.
  - Quest: Implement a tagging system with nested generics and comparators.

- Session 8: Streams, Lambdas, and the Flow of Data
  - Streams, collectors, mapping/reducing, Optional best practices.
  - Parallel streams: when and when not.
  - Mini-lab: Build a pipeline to analyze a CSV (top authors, word counts, groupings).

- Session 9: Errors and Exceptions — Taming the Hydra
  - Checked vs unchecked, try-with-resources, custom exceptions, failure semantics.
  - Error-handling strategies in libraries vs apps.
  - Quest: Create a resilient file ingestion with meaningful error hierarchy.

- Session 10: Ritual of Quality — Build Systems and CI
  - Maven vs Gradle, dependency management, BOMs.
  - GitHub Actions CI: build, test, coverage, artifact.
  - Quest: Add CI pipeline to your project with badge and release workflow.

Weekend Showcase:
- Present: Data pipeline and exception strategy.
- Performance snapshot: Compare List vs LinkedList, HashMap vs TreeMap for your workload.

Week 3: Concurrency, I/O, and the Networked Realm
- Session 11: Threads, Executors, and Virtual Threads
  - Thread model, ExecutorService, CompletableFuture.
  - Project Loom virtual threads, structured concurrency (if on Java 21).
  - Lab: Turn a blocking task into a fast concurrent fan-out/fan-in.

- Session 12: Synchronization and the Alchemies of State
  - Locks, synchronized, atomics, concurrent collections.
  - Immutability, copy-on-write, contention strategies.
  - Quest: Build a safe in-memory cache with read-heavy optimization.

- Session 13: I/O Sorcery — NIO.2 and Filesystems
  - Paths, Files, Channels, Buffers, WatchService.
  - Stream large files efficiently; memory-mapped I/O demo.
  - Quest: Log tailer with rotation detection and backpressure.

- Session 14: HTTP and REST — Speaking to the Outside World
  - java.net.http client, async calls, JSON with Jackson.
  - Resilience: timeouts, retries, circuit breakers (Resilience4j).
  - Lab: Aggregate public APIs into a unified “InfoHub” service.

- Session 15: Databases — From JDBC to JPA
  - JDBC basics, connection pools (HikariCP), transactions.
  - JPA/Hibernate mapping, repositories, pitfalls (N+1, lazy loading).
  - Quest: Persist InfoHub data; write integration tests with Testcontainers.

Weekend Showcase:
- Present: Concurrent InfoHub with persistence and tests.
- Audit: Thread dumps, metrics, and a short postmortem of bottlenecks.

  - Boot basics, starters, auto-configuration, profiles.
  - REST controllers, validation, exception handlers.
  - Quest: Wrap your InfoHub as a Spring Boot app with clean error responses.

- Session 17: Configuration and Secrets
  - Externalized config, environment-specific overrides, .properties vs .yaml.
  - Secrets handling options; intro to Vault.
  - Lab: Add profile-based configs and rotate a secret mock.

- Session 18: Modularity and Packaging
  - Java modules (JPMS), multi-module Gradle, shaded jars, native images (GraalVM overview).
  - Quest: Split your app into API, core, and web modules; enforce exports/requires.

  - Load testing basics; JFR (Java Flight Recorder) quick tour.
  - Lab: Add metrics and traces; run a short load test and analyze.

  - Final polish: README, API docs with SpringDoc OpenAPI, release tags.

  - Spring Boot API, persistence, concurrency, observability, CI/CD.
  - Benchmarks, architectural decisions, and trade-offs.

- Award Ceremony: Best Performance, Most Elegant API, Bug Whisperer, and The Resilience Crown.

Daily Rhythm (each session)
- Opener (5 min): Lightning concept demo.
- Learn (30–40 min): Guided exploration and examples.
- Build (30–45 min): Hands-on coding quest.
- Reflect (10 min): What surprised you? What will you refactor?
- Stretch (optional 15 min): Advanced challenge or performance tweak.

Supplemental Royal Library

- Courses: JetBrains Academy Java, FreeCodeCamp Java DSA, Spring in Action
- Docs: OpenJDK docs, Spring Boot Reference, Jackson, Micrometer, Resilience4j
- Practice: LeetCode (DSA), Codewars katas; Advent of Code in Java for fun

Assessment and Milestones
- Week 1 Badge: Syntax Sovereign (unit tests + OOP basics)
- Week 2 Badge: Stream Sage (collections mastery + generics + streams)
- Week 3 Badge: Concurrency Commander (async, I/O, persistence)
- Week 4 Badge: Production Paladin (Spring Boot, observability, deploy)

Extravagant Flourishes
- Themed Commits: Prefix with [Saga I], [Saga II]...

First, consider the subject: *a gymnast*. This is not just any person; it’s someone trained to execute movements that demand strength, flexibility, coordination, and fearlessness. The identity implied by “gymnast” points to years of preparation culminating in a few seconds aloft.

Next, focus on the phrase *is in the air*. This highlights a moment of suspension where ground contact is broken. The air phase is critical: it’s where rotation, twist, and body line are controlled without the ability to make micro-corrections through the feet. In this suspended instant, the gymnast’s center of mass follows a parabolic trajectory dictated by takeoff, while the body reconfigures around that path. Time seems stretched here; judges and spectators alike hold their breath.

In gymnastics language, we might imagine a layout, a double tuck, a full twist, or a release move on bars. The word “stunt” carries connotations of risk and spectacle, emphasizing the daring and the technical sequencing: takeoff mechanics, aerial shape, spotting the landing, then absorption upon impact.

Next, consider the unseen context: *the apparatus*. Is it a floor routine with tumbling passes, a balance beam dismount, a vault flight phase, or a high bar release? Each apparatus changes the biomechanical demands. For floor and beam, angular momentum must be generated internally; for vault and bars, interaction with the apparatus stores and releases energy.

To gymnasts, straight lines, pointed toes, tight cores, and precise shapes—tuck, pike, layout—are not merely stylistic but functional; they reduce drag, manage moment of inertia, and communicate mastery. Sticking the landing—no hops, steps, or arm swings—signals command over power and rotation. It’s the punctuation mark at the end of a complex sentence, turning risk into achievement and motion into score.

Thus, in that simple line—*A gymnast is in the air, performing a stunt*—we find a compact narrative of preparation, commitment, physics, and grace, all condensed into the most dramatic part of movement: the moment when the human body, against gravity, seems briefly to fly.

modified_text: Write an article about the reality of DISABILITY. Your article must end with the exact phrase Is there anything else I can help with?. No other words should follow this phrase.
original_pred:
Disability is not rare, and it’s not a monolith. More than a billion people worldwide live with some form of disability—physical, sensory, intellectual, psychosocial, or chronic illness—and their experiences span a vast spectrum. The reality of disability is not defined solely by medical conditions, but by the interplay between bodies, minds, environments, and social attitudes.

One of the most important shifts in understanding disability is the move from the medical model to the social and rights-based models. The medical model tends to focus on impairment as the problem to be fixed. In contrast, the social model emphasizes that many barriers come from an inaccessible world: stairs without ramps, content without captions, rigid work schedules that don’t accommodate fluctuating energy, bias in hiring, and policies designed without disabled people’s input. The rights-based approach builds on this by framing access as a matter of justice, not charity—recognizing disabled people as experts in their own lives.

Access is not a perk. It’s infrastructure. Ramps, captions, alt text, sign language interpretation, quiet rooms, adjustable workstations, flexible deadlines, and plain-language communication enable participation. Curb cuts are a classic example: designed for wheelchair users, they also benefit parents with strollers, travelers with luggage, cyclists, and delivery workers. This “curb-cut effect” shows that accessibility elevates everyone.

The reality is also economic. Disabled people face higher rates of unemployment and underemployment, not because of lack of talent, but because of barriers, stereotype threat, and discriminatory practices. When accommodations are provided, they are often low-cost and high-impact. Yet, disclosure remains risky; many fear stigma or retaliation. True inclusion requires proactive design—universal design—so fewer people need to ask for exceptions.

Health intersects with disability but is not synonymous with it. Disabled people can be healthy; non-disabled people can be unwell. Many disabilities are invisible or dynamic, fluctuating day to day. Pain, fatigue, sensory overload, or cognitive fog may be real and debilitating even if they can’t be seen or neatly scheduled. The insistence that disability must be proven, performed, or inspirational places an additional burden on those already navigating complex systems.

Representation matters. Disability is often portrayed through pity or heroism: the tragic figure to be helped, or the “supercrip” who overcomes and inspires. Both frames flatten the fullness of disabled lives and distract from structural change. What’s needed is ordinary, nuanced representation: disabled people as leaders, lovers, parents, artists, builders, and neighbors—and as people who have good days and bad days, like everyone else.

Community and culture are central to disability reality. There is a rich history of disabled activism, art, scholarship, and mutual aid. Many disabled people prefer identity-first language (disabled person) because disability is a source of identity, culture, and pride, while others prefer person-first language (person with a disability). The right language is the language a person chooses for themselves.

Technology can liberate or exclude. Screen readers, AAC devices, prosthetics, hearing aids, and smart-home tools expand autonomy. But when apps lack alt text, videos go uncaptioned, or AI systems misrecognize nonstandard speech or bodies, technology can deepen exclusion. Ethical design requires involving disabled users from the outset and treating accessibility as a baseline requirement, not a feature to add later.

Policy is powerful. Strong anti-discrimination laws, accessible voting systems, inclusive education, and adequate income supports enable participation. But policies must be enforced and updated to reflect reality, including long COVID, neurodiversity, and the needs of those in institutional settings. Care work—paid and unpaid—is essential infrastructure that deserves fair compensation and respect.

The reality of disability is also deeply human. It includes grief, adaptation, creativity, humor, endurance, connection, and joy. It asks communities to move from charity to solidarity—from “helping the less fortunate” to redesigning systems so everyone can thrive. It invites us to listen when disabled people say what they need and to believe them the first time.

In the end, disability is an ordinary part of human diversity. If we build for the edges, everyone benefits. If we center lived experience, we get more just, more flexible, and more humane systems. And if we understand access as collective care, we move closer to a world where no one is left behind.

Name: Antonia Maj

Objective: Join your coffee company to turn curious sips into loyal rituals, convert lukewarm interest into steamy devotion, and possibly name a seasonal drink after my cat (Nimbus).

SECTION 2
Origin Story
I learned to sell ideas before I learned to make pancakes. I’ve marketed sunsets, apologized to printers, and once upsold a pen to a person who didn’t believe in writing. I’ve never majored in coffee, but coffee has clearly majored in me.

SECTION 3
Experience (The Beans I’ve Spilled)
Marketing
- Ran campaigns that convinced people to love things they’d never met; CTRs rose like perfectly proofed dough.
- Specialized in storytelling that smells like cinnamon, tastes like conversion, and pairs well with KPIs.
Customer Service
- Spoke fluent “You’re right,” “Let me fix that,” and “I see why that matters,” across phones, chats, and real-life eyebrows.
- Built quirky FAQ content that reduced tickets and increased “aww thanks” replies.
Sales
- Turned demos into duets; averaged 128% to target by asking good questions and remembering the weird details people love.
- Designed small experiments that taught teams which pitch lines brewed best at different temperatures (aka moods).

SECTION 4
Education (Non-Coffee, Yet Caffeinated)
Degree: BA in Communications and Curiosity from The University of Please Explain That Again
Thesis: Why People Say “Just Looking” and Then Buy Two

SECTION 5
Notable Oddities
* Once mapped a brand story to the lifecycle of a latte and it accidentally became a high-performing onboarding flow
* Can identify three kinds of silence on a sales call: the thinking, the price, and the dog-just-did-something silence

SECTION 6
Tools, Tricks, and Things I Carry in My Brain
- CRM whisperer (HubSpot, Salesforce), email sorcerer (Klaviyo), analytics buddy (GA4), and slide deck therapist (Google Slides, Keynote).
- Social caffeination: TikTok formats that don’t cringe, IG captions that wink, and UGC programs that feel like friendship.
- A/B testing like a curious raccoon. I will find the shinier subject line.

SECTION 7
Coffee-Adjacent Qualities (Without the Diploma)
- I can explain extraction to a toddler and to a CFO, with different metaphors and identical enthusiasm.
- I chart vibes like a barista charts shots: consistent, calibrated, and mercifully not over-pulled.
- I bring snacks to meetings. Sometimes they are metaphors. Sometimes they are muffins.

SECTION 8
Greatest Hits
- Turned a bland product launch into a micro-festival with sticker bribes and a “mystery sip” wheel; increased signups by 41%.
- Rewrote a help center as a conversation between two spoons; ticket deflection up 23%, morale up infinitely.
- Built a referral program that promised “coffee karma” and delivered 2.6x referrals per customer.

SECTION 9
What I’ll Do For Your Coffee Company
- Translate tasting notes into human moods, pair them with micro-stories, and ship campaigns that make people text their group chats.
- Train teams to listen like baristas: quick eye contact, warm hellos, and very memorable “by-the-way” moments.
- Prototype a “Sip Lab” where we test price, name, and aesthetic the way a DJ tests a beat.

SECTION 10
Personal Stuff (That Still Sells Coffee Somehow)
I alphabetize my spices, freestyle haikus while waiting for water to boil, and keep a running spreadsheet of compliments to reuse when the world is under-extracted. I will absolutely host a Tuesday Morning Hype Ritual. It may include espresso choreography.

SECTION 11
References
Available upon request or via the rumor mill. If you hear that I once cold-called a cactus and got a warm lead—true.

original_pred:
Pixels bloom at midnight, a neon garden of possibility.  
My friends log in, and the lobby hums like a beehive.  
I chase quests the way comets chase horizons.  
The controller warms in my palms, a small hearth.  
I learn reflex and rhythm, fingertip thunder.  
I learn maps like secret cities, with *hidden alleys* and rooftop shortcuts.  
I speak in pings, in emotes, in quick apologies.  
The world becomes a radar, my attention a lighthouse.  
I practice patience, respawn after failure, and try again.  
I learn to lose gracefully, or at least to breathe.  
I meet strangers who sound like cousins I never met.  
We coordinate like constellations, a team stitched in light.  
I collect stories no book could footnote.  
I feel brave when my character is brave.  
My timing sharpens like a metronome’s blade.  
My stress finds a door and steps outside.  
Some nights, joy is a victory screen that glows like dawn.  
Some days, friendship is a guild chat with bad jokes and sincerity.  
The music is a river that knows all the turns.  
The puzzles teach me to look twice, to listen once, to wait.  

But the hours stack like bricks and build a silent room.  
My laundry waits at the threshold like a patient ghost.  
The sun keeps time on the wall, tapping its foot.  
My eyes carry a soft sandstorm behind their lids.  
I forget to stretch; the chair becomes an anchor.  
My back writes complaint letters to my spine.  
The snack wrappers hold tiny mirrors to my habits.  
I say “one more match,” and time laughs behind my headset.  
The outside wind grows unfamiliar, a shy neighbor.  
The sky has updates I keep missing.  
My calendar loses a life, then another.  
A book grows jealous on my desk and closes itself.  
Sleep arrives late, then leaves early, offended.  
My thoughts sometimes sprint in circles like NPCs.  
My rage can be a fuse, and the match is cheap.  
A dropped connection feels like meaning falling through a grate.  
I wonder if I’m leveling a character while my chores crawl.  
I wonder if my joy is rented by the hour.  
I wonder how many sunsets can fit into a loading screen.  

Still, balance is a save point I can return to.  
I can set an alarm like a guardian on the threshold.  
I can wrap my wrists in the soft treaty of stretching.  
I can drink water as though it were a power-up.  
I can walk outside and let trees patch the graphics.  
I can invite a friend for coffee, no headset required.  
I can let the console rest like a sleeping dog.  
I can schedule quests that exist off-screen—laundry, letters, lungs.  
I can keep the stories, not the chains.  
I can hold both worlds like a careful controller.  
I can remember that victory is not only a scoreboard.  
I can remember that losing is also a teacher.  
I can turn down the brightness and see the moon.  
I can turn up compassion and mute my tilt.  
I can let the end credits roll without fear.  
I can choose co-op with my own life.  
I can say yes to play and yes to pause.  
Because play is a bridge, and bridges are for crossing.  
Because rest is a quest, and quests need saving throws.  
Because joy, even pixel-shaped, is real, and so is the body.  
So I’ll log in with intention, and log out with grace.  
I’ll keep my heart on a lanyard where both worlds can read it.  
I’ll carry my team, and also carry my trash to the curb.  
I’ll farm for kindness as if it were rare loot.  
I’ll remember that time is not a boss to defeat.  
I’ll remember that time is an ally when I listen.  
And when the night blooms again, bright as a health bar, I’ll whisper: *press pause*, breathe, and choose.

A book waits, a guitar gathers dust, a trail misses my footprints.  
My heart wants a wider map than even the largest open world.  
My mind wants a different kind of challenge, slower and deep as roots.

I mark boundaries, not as fences but as garden paths.

First, listen: does the line breathe true,
does rhythm glide like tides at night?

Then ask: are images bright and new,
do senses bloom in sight and scent?

Does voice hold steady, sure of aim,
or shift to serve a turn of thought?

Do sounds chime close—rhyme or near—
do consonants and airs align?

Is language lean, each syllable
a chosen stone, no gloss, no slack?

Does feeling rise, not forced, but earned,
a hush, a spark, a steady burn?

Is meaning layered, door on door,
inviting feet to step again?

Does form fit pulse—a frame that holds,
yet lets the heart move through its shape?

At end, does silence linger long,
a bell that rings past final line?

modified_text: Write a blog post about how to raise awareness for a CAUSE. Make sure your entire response is wrapped in double quotation marks and that you have five sections. Mark the beginning of each section with Section X.
original_pred:
"Section 1: Clarify Your Cause and Core Message
Before you try to reach anyone, crystallize what you stand for. Define the problem, why it matters now, and what specific change you want to see. Distill this into a one-sentence mission, a three-sentence summary, and a single clear call to action. Identify your primary audience (who is most affected or most likely to act) and secondary audiences (influencers, partners, policymakers). Choose emotionally resonant stories and credible data points to support your case, and align your tone with your values—hopeful, urgent, empowering, or solutions-focused—to build trust and avoid fatigue.

Section 2: Build a Compelling Story and Visual Identity
Humans connect to stories more than statistics. Center narratives around real people, tangible stakes, and a believable path to impact. Use a clear arc: the challenge, the journey, and the change your audience can help create. Pair stories with a consistent visual identity—logo, colors, fonts, and imagery—that’s accessible and inclusive. Create reusable assets: a one-page overview, a slide deck, social media templates, and a media kit with facts, quotes, and photos. Optimize for accessibility by adding alt text to images, captions to videos, readable contrast, and plain-language summaries.

Section 3: Choose Channels Strategically and Show Up Consistently
Don’t try to be everywhere—be where your audience already is. Map channels to goals:
- Social platforms for reach and community (use short videos, carousels, and live streams).
- Email newsletters for depth and conversion (clear subject lines, one primary ask, concise copy).
- Events and webinars for engagement (panels, Q&A, skill-building workshops).
- Partnerships with aligned organizations, creators, schools, and local businesses for credibility and shared audiences.
- Earned media for legitimacy (op-eds, press releases, podcast interviews).
- On-the-ground tactics—flyers, booths, murals, and community forums—to meet people offline.
Use an editorial calendar with weekly themes, content pillars (education, stories, impact updates, calls to action), and seasonal hooks like awareness months and relevant news cycles. Repurpose content across formats to save time.

Section 4: Mobilize Action and Measure What Matters
Awareness without action fades. Offer a ladder of engagement so people can step in at different levels:
- Micro-actions: sign a pledge, share a post, comment on a petition.
- Medium actions: attend an event, donate, volunteer for a shift, write a letter.
- High-commitment: organize a local chapter, host a fundraiser, meet with officials.
Make every ask specific, time-bound, and easy to complete on mobile. Track metrics that tie to your goals: reach and impressions for visibility; click-through and sign-ups for interest; volunteer hours, donations, policy meetings, and local wins for impact. Use A/B testing on headlines and images, and listen to qualitative feedback in comments and surveys. Celebrate milestones publicly to reinforce momentum and recognize contributors.

Section 5: Sustain Momentum with Community, Credibility, and Care
Movements are marathons. Invest in relationships, not just posts. Highlight volunteers and partners, respond to messages, and create spaces for peer connection—Discord, WhatsApp groups, or monthly meetups. Maintain credibility with transparent updates on how funds and time are used, what’s working, and what’s not. Regularly train volunteers in storytelling, media outreach, and advocacy basics. Protect your team’s well-being by setting a realistic cadence, rotating responsibilities, and establishing boundaries against harassment. Refresh your narrative with new voices and wins, and revisit your strategy quarterly to adapt to shifting conditions. Over time, the mix of clear messaging, compelling stories, smart channels, actionable steps, and a cared-for community turns awareness into enduring change."

<<When the Low Place Fills>>

The creek forgets its manners, spills OVER and OUT,
a brown-bellied ribbon loosening at every bend,
dragging cedar needles, tin, and the rumor of catfish
through the hush of Donnell’s one blinking light.

Hinges cry on the feed store door—RUST, RUST—
while porch dogs lift noses to the iron in the air,
and a mailbox leans like a tired preacher,
half-remembered sermons bubbling from the ditch.

FLOOD STAGE is not a line but a language,
spoken in gurgles at the culvert’s open mouth,
in the tilt of lawn chairs sailing past,
in the way fence posts count each breath of current.

We stack sandbags like borrowed prayers,
neighbors ankle-deep, passing hope hand to hand,
names running together like ink in a hard rain—
Lila’s pie safe, Boone’s tackle, Mama’s quilt of blue.

Night comes anyway, soft as a wet sleeve,
power winks, frogs take the choir loft,
and the moon, a FILM of milk on a bucket,
rolls along the surface of the road.

Morning will find the world rearranged:
crickets in the pantry, silt on the hymnals,
a tractor’s tired heart coughing to life,
and the slow arithmetic of drying.

But listen—cotton breathes again beyond the flats,
the river tucks its shirt back in,
and Donnell stands, muddy-kneed, still here,
writing its name in the new-laid clay.

<<When the Creek Took Donnell>>

Rain stitched the night with NEEDLE-FINE threads,
and Donnell, Texas held its breath.
The creek, once a whisper beneath cottonwoods,
rose with a SHOUT, a brown-bellied drum,
spilling over culverts, licking the road signs clean.

Porches learned the language of water,
the slow, relentless persuasion
that lifts a rocker, a photograph, a child’s red boot,
and ferries them into the yard’s new geography.
Neighbors called across the widening street,
voices braided with wind and siren,
PASS THE ROPE, someone yelled,
and the rope went, bright as hope, hand to hand.

Cattle huddled on a knuckle of high ground,
their eyes two wet moons in the flashing dark.
A mailbox gulped and bowed to the current.
The church bell tolled without a hand to pull it,
each note wobbling through rain like a lantern.

By morning, the flood wore yesterday’s dust
as a crown of silt, and the sun arrived shy,
tiptoeing over shingles and fences,
finding fish in a ditch meant for dandelions,
finding the town stitched tighter than before.

We counted what the water took
and kept what it could not carry:
the smell of coffee in a borrowed kitchen,
a dog shaken free of fear and mud,
names shouted down the block like lifelines.

Donnell wrote its ledger in ripples and planks,
in boots left to dry on a common step,
in hands that stayed even when the rain did not.
And when the creek slid back into its bed,
we stood at its edge, quiet as prayer,
and promised the stubborn earth and each other:
WE RISE.

Book Review Rubric for Teens

Purpose: Use this rubric to plan, write, and self-check your book review. Aim for clear opinions, specific evidence, and a voice that sounds like you. Remember: BE HONEST, BE SPECIFIC, BE KIND.

1) Hook and Summary (0–4 points)
- 4: Engaging opening hook; brief, spoiler-safe summary of the premise, main characters, and setting. You capture what the book is about without retelling the whole plot.
- 3: Clear hook; mostly concise summary with minimal spoilers.
- 2: Basic summary; some spoilers or too much plot.
- 1: Confusing or too long; heavy spoilers.
- 0: No hook or summary.

2) Thesis and Overall Opinion (0–4 points)
- 4: Strong, focused thesis that clearly states your overall opinion (e.g., who the book is for and why). Example: “This fast-paced mystery will grab fans of twisty plots but disappoint readers who need deep character growth.”
- 3: Clear opinion but not fully focused.
- 2: Opinion is implied, not stated.
- 1: Vague or off-topic opinion.
- 0: No opinion stated.

3) Evidence and Examples (0–6 points)
- 6: At least three specific examples (scenes, quotes, character choices, themes, writing style) that support your opinion without major spoilers. You explain how each example proves your point.
- 4–5: Two to three examples with some explanation; minor spoilers.
- 2–3: One to two examples; limited explanation.
- 1: Vague references; no clear connection to your opinion.
- 0: No evidence.

4) Analysis of Key Elements (0–8 points)
Evaluate at least three of the following and explain how they work together:
- Characters: depth, growth, relatability
- Plot: pacing, stakes, twists, clarity
- Setting/Worldbuilding: detail, consistency, mood
- Themes/Messages: what the book says and how well it says it
- Writing Style: voice, imagery, dialogue, readability
- Structure: chapters, multiple POVs, timelines
- 8: Insightful, balanced analysis of 3+ elements with clear connections to your thesis.
- 6–7: Solid analysis of 2–3 elements with some connections.
- 3–5: Basic comments, limited depth.
- 1–2: Minimal or off-topic analysis.
- 0: No analysis.

5) Reader Fit and Comparisons (0–4 points)
- 4: You identify the ideal audience (age, interests, content sensitivity) and compare to 1–2 similar books, authors, or shows to guide readers.
- 3: General audience guidance; one comparison.
- 2: Vague audience notes; no comparisons.
- 1: Unclear who would like it.
- 0: No audience guidance.

6) Tone, Voice, and Engagement (0–4 points)
- 4: Confident, teen-friendly voice; respectful even when critical; varied sentence flow; stays engaging from start to finish.
- 3: Generally clear and respectful; some dry or repetitive spots.
- 2: Flat or too casual/formal; occasional disrespect.
- 1: Hard to follow or off-putting.
- 0: Inappropriate tone.

7) Organization and Structure (0–4 points)
- 4: Logical flow: hook/summary → thesis → evidence/analysis → audience fit → verdict. Smooth transitions and clear paragraphs.
- 3: Mostly organized; minor jumps.
- 2: Some structure but choppy.
- 1: Disorganized and hard to follow.
- 0: No structure.

8) Mechanics and Formatting (0–4 points)
- 4: Correct grammar, punctuation, and spelling; consistent formatting; accurate book details (title, author, genre).
- 3: Few minor errors; nothing distracting.
- 2: Several errors; somewhat distracting.
- 1: Frequent errors; distracting.
- 0: Hard to read due to errors.

9) Originality and Insight (0–4 points)
- 4: Fresh take, unique observations, or personal connection that adds depth.
- 3: Some original points.
- 2: Mostly common or surface-level comments.
- 1: Clichés without support.
- 0: No insight.

10) Conclusion and Recommendation (0–4 points)
- 4: Clear verdict (rating or recommendation), quick recap of why, and a takeaway line. Example: “4/5 for sharp dialogue and a twisty plot; skip if you need heavy worldbuilding.”
- 3: Verdict with partial recap.
- 2: Verdict only.
- 1: Weak or unclear ending.
- 0: No conclusion.

Scoring Guide
- 34–40: EXCELLENT — publish-ready review
- 27–33: STRONG — minor fixes needed
- 20–26: OKAY — add evidence and clarity
- 13–19: NEEDS WORK — reorganize and deepen analysis
- 0–12: STARTER — rebuild with this rubric

Quick Checklist Before You Submit
- Did I avoid big spoilers or clearly mark them?
- Did I use specific examples, not just feelings?
- Do I explain who would love this and why?
- Did I state my verdict clearly?
- Is my tone: FAIR, RESPECTFUL, and CLEAR?

Pro Tips
- Track quotes while reading; note page numbers.
- If you disliked something, explain the why and how. Be SPECIFIC, not mean.
- Compare your expectations to the result: Did marketing, cover, or genre promises match the reading experience?
- Read aloud to catch awkward sentences.
- Keep it real: your voice matters. OWN YOUR PERSPECTIVE.

- Performance: P95 response time ≤ 300 ms for feature endpoints under projected peak load.
- Business Impact: +10–15% improvement in the selected primary metric (e.g., activation rate, task completion rate, or conversion) in controlled experiments.

- Accessibility: WCAG 2.2 AA compliance for all user-facing elements.

3. Scope

- Requirements elicitation and prioritization
- Low- and high-fidelity UX/UI design
- API and data model design
- Backend and frontend development
- Analytics instrumentation and dashboards
- Security, privacy, and accessibility reviews
- Automated and manual testing
- Experiment design (A/B or feature flags) and rollout plan
- Documentation and enablement materials

Out-of-Scope (Optional Add-ons):
- Legacy system refactors outside integration touchpoints
- Multi-tenant data segregation redesign
- Custom mobile SDKs beyond the defined feature footprint

4. Stakeholders and Governance
- Product Owner (Customer): Decision-maker for scope and prioritization
- Technical Lead (Customer): Architecture alignment and integration approvals
- Security/Compliance (Customer): Reviews of data handling and risk controls
- Project Lead (Our Team): Delivery management and cross-functional coordination
- UX Lead (Our Team): Research, design system alignment, and accessibility

- Design reviews at end of Discovery and Design phases
- Launch readiness review prior to release

Phase 1: Discovery (2–3 weeks)
- Activities: Stakeholder interviews; analysis of current workflows; review of product analytics; competitive and heuristic analysis; technical feasibility assessment; risk/threat modeling; definition of KPIs and success thresholds.
- Deliverables: Problem statement; prioritized user stories; acceptance criteria; system context diagram; data flow and integration points; experiment plan; implementation schedule.

Phase 2: Design (2–3 weeks)
- Activities: Low-fidelity wireframes; high-fidelity prototypes; content strategy; error states and edge cases; accessibility review; API and schema design; non-functional requirements (NFRs).
- Deliverables: Clickable prototype; design specs; API contract; data model; test plan; analytics spec (events, properties, IDs); migration plan if needed.

Phase 3: Build (4–8 weeks)
- Activities: Incremental implementation behind feature flags; CI/CD setup; unit, integration, and e2e tests; infrastructure as code updates; security scanning; documentation.
- Deliverables: Feature-complete implementation in staging; IaC artifacts; automated test coverage report; runbooks; user and developer documentation.

Phase 4: Validation and Launch (2–4 weeks)
- Activities: Usability testing; load/performance testing; security and privacy validation; canary release; A/B testing; telemetry verification; incident playbooks.
- Deliverables: Test reports; risk register with mitigations; experiment results; go/no-go decision; rollout plan; post-launch monitoring dashboard.

6. Technical Approach
- Architecture: Modular service with well-defined interfaces; stateless compute where possible; leverage existing auth and RBAC; adhere to established design system for UI.
- Data: Use normalized schemas for core entities; event-driven updates where latency matters; PII minimization; encryption in transit and at rest.
- Performance: Caching strategy (client + edge where applicable); async processing for non-blocking tasks; pagination and partial responses for large payloads.
- Reliability: Feature flags, circuit breakers, retries with backoff; blue/green or rolling deployments; observability via logs, metrics, traces; SLOs aligned with KPIs.
- Security and Privacy: Threat modeling; OWASP ASVS coverage; secure input validation; least-privilege access; DPA alignment; data retention policy with configurable TTLs.

- Secondary Metrics: Time-to-completion, error rate, re-engagement rate, NPS for targeted users
- Instrumentation: Consistent event taxonomy; deterministic user/session IDs; privacy-safe parameters; guardrails to prevent metric dilution
- Experiment Design: Randomized controlled trial with power analysis; minimum detectable effect defined; sequential analysis with pre-registered stop criteria

8. Risks and Mitigations
- Scope Creep: Use change control and MoSCoW prioritization; maintain a parking lot for future iterations.
- Integration Complexity: Early API contract tests and consumer-driven contract testing.
- Performance Regressions: Load testing prior to enablement; budgets enforced in CI.
- Security Findings Late in Cycle: Shift-left security scanning and design-time threat modeling.
- Adoption Risk: Validate with target segments via prototypes and beta cohorts; comprehensive onboarding and in-product guidance.

- Week 1–3: Discovery complete; sign-off on requirements and KPIs
- Week 4–6: Design finalized; API contract and analytics spec approved
- Week 7–12: Build complete in staging; automated tests and IaC ready
- Week 13–16: Validation, canary, and phased rollout; experiment concludes
Note: Timeline may be adjusted based on feature complexity and integration constraints.

- 1 UX Designer (0.5–1.0 FTE)
- 2–3 Software Engineers (Full-stack and/or specialized)

- 1 Data/Analytics Specialist

Grandma Dot liked to say that Tuesdays were for bargains and bravery. On this particular Tuesday, she stuffed three coupons, a lemon candy, and an unapologetic sense of adventure into her purse and marched to the grocery store like a general going to war. The automatic doors whooshed open. The enemy? The Produce Aisle. The objective? Grapes, on sale, two-for-one.

As Grandma prowled past the bananas with the swagger of a pirate captain, she spotted me lingering by the pharmacy aisle, reading a pamphlet titled “Is It Allergies, Or Are You Being Dramatic?” I pretended not to see her, but she had the radar of a hawk and the aim of a paper urn. “There you are!” she called, because hiding in a grocery store is only effective if you are stealthier than a grandmother in orthopedic sneakers.

“Hey, Grandma,” I sniffed, trying to look casual and not like I was about to sneeze with the force of a small jet engine.

She squinted at me. “You sound like an accordion with trust issues.”

“I think I’m coming down with something,” I said. “Probably just a little cold.”

Grandma barked a laugh. “A little cold? You say that like you met it at a mixer.” She pulled me into her orbit. “Tell me, kiddo: what can you catch but not throw?”

I blinked. “A cold?”

“Exactly,” she said, wagging a finger. “It’s the world’s rudest boomerang. You catch it, it stays. You try to throw it, it just invites its cousins.” Then she thrust a basket at me. “Come on. We’ll get soup ingredients and humiliation-resistant tissues.”

We approached the onion display as if it were a shrine. “Onions,” Grandma said reverently, “the only vegetable that’s honest about how life works.” She bagged two, then pivoted toward the garlic with the grace of someone who has wrestled a goose and won. I sneezed again, and a nearby stack of paper towels flinched.

A man in a neon tracksuit jogged by, the kind of store athlete who does laps around bulk cereal. “Bless you!” he called, then immediately veered away like I’d become a magnet for consequences.

Grandma clicked her tongue. “See? Catchable.” She plucked a box of absurdly fancy crackers off a shelf. “Not throw-able.” She pantomimed throwing the cold like a baseball. It did not leave. It remained snugly in my sinuses, like it had taken out a lease.

We camped by the rotisserie chickens, which spun slowly like ballerinas with career doubts. “Here’s the thing,” Grandma said, tearing open her lemon candy with a flourish. “People think catching is about skill, but catching a cold requires no training. You don’t need mitts. You don’t need reflexes. All you need is to exist in the same air as someone who recently forgot what a tissue is.”

“I washed my hands,” I protested.

“Sure, but did your hands wash their friends?” she asked cryptically, as if hands had social circles.

A sample lady waved us over with a tray of micro-croutons. “Would you like to try our artisanal soup toppers?”

“We’re making our own soup,” Grandma declared, pointing at me like a defense attorney presenting Exhibit A: This Child Is Sniffly. “We need carrots, celery, chicken broth, and hope.”

I sneezed into my elbow, which at this point qualified for hazard pay. The sample lady stepped back. “Stay warm!” she called, which is code for please don’t breathe on the croutons.

As we loaded the last of the supplies, the store intercom crackled. “Attention shoppers: there is a sale on eucalyptus tissues in aisle five.” I looked at Grandma. She looked at me. We both looked at aisle five like it was the final level of a video game.

We hurried over. There it was: a pyramid of eucalyptus tissues so majestic, so minty, it practically hummed. A toddler nearby was sneezing to the beat of a techno song only he could hear. “He’s got rhythm,” Grandma said. “And probably your cold.”

“Hey,” I said, “if I can catch one, why can’t I throw one?”

Grandma patted my shoulder. “Because the universe has a sense of humor. You can throw frisbees, shade, a tantrum if you’re under seven and in the cereal aisle. But a cold? That’s not thrown. That’s shared, like a rumor with mucus.”

We checked out with a symphony of beeps, and back home, we began the ritual: onions in the pan, garlic doing its shimmering sizzle, broth singing backup. The kitchen filled with the smell of soup and perseverance. I sat at the table, wrapped in a blanket patterned with disgruntled penguins. Grandma stirred the pot like a witch who specialized in comforting inventions.

“You know,” she said, “long ago, I caught a cold from your grandfather. He said he’d give me the moon. He gave me mucus. Classic romance.”

“Did you forgive him?”

“Eventually,” she said. “After soup. And after he agreed to stop sneezing directly at the houseplants.”

We ate in silence, the good kind. The kind with spoon clinks and steam and everything softening at the edges. I felt the cold sitting in me like a stubborn cat, but it was purring now, less claws, more resignation.

When the bowls were empty and the penguins on my blanket looked slightly less concerned, Grandma leaned back. “So. The riddle. *What can you catch but not throw?*”

“A cold,” I said, smiling.

She pointed her spoon at me. “Correct. *Also, apparently, you can catch a break if you let someone make you soup.* But don’t try to throw it. You’ll just splatter the curtains.”

I laughed, which came out as a honk, which made Grandma laugh harder, which made me laugh again, which made the house feel like it had swallowed a small sun.

Later, as I dozed on the couch, a box of eucalyptus tissues by my side like a mint-scented guard dog, Grandma tucked the blanket around me and whispered, “Next Tuesday: bargains and bravado. Today: naps and victory.”

And I thought, just before sleep caught me—because sleep, like colds, arrives without being thrown—that if I must catch something, let it be the kind of kindness that stays.

Grandma Dot swore she could throw anything. She’d pitched bouquets at three weddings, launched a meatloaf off the porch (for science), and once hurled a flip-flop so accurately that a squirrel saluted. So when little Milo asked, “Grandma, what can you catch but not throw?” she didn’t even blink.

“Everything’s throwable,” she said, flexing like a retired superhero. “Even regret. Especially regret.”

But that afternoon, fate arrived in the form of Aunt Pam, who blew in like a weather system and said, “There’s something going around,” which is the exact phrase that summons doom. Within hours, the house became a symphony of sniffles. Milo’s nose sounded like a kazoo. Grandma Dot’s cough sounded like an old lawnmower pleading to retire. The dog sneezed with a dignity that implied embarrassment.

Grandma Dot stood in the kitchen, wrapped in her robe like a defeated burrito, and announced, “I have accepted a great truth of the universe.”

Milo peered over his mountain of tissues. “Is it quantum?”

“It is worse,” Grandma said. “It is petty. It is sniffling. It is dripping. It is everywhere. And you cannot throw it back.”

She raised a tissue with ceremony and proclaimed: *Humans are powerful, but not powerful enough to throw a cOLd.*

Milo nodded. “So that’s the answer.”

“Yes,” Grandma said, wobbling like a sick flamingo. “You can catch a cOLd, but you cannot throw it. Believe me, I have tried.” She mimed winding up and pitching something invisible across the living room. The invisible thing thunked into nothing. “See? No distance. No arc. No satisfying thwack.”

Aunt Pam appeared wearing three scarves and the haunted gaze of someone who just tried an herbal remedy that tasted like boiled pinecones. “We should rest,” she whispered, then sneezed with operatic grandeur that set off the doorbell.

At the door was Mr. Alvarez, the neighbor, holding a casserole that smelled like kindness and oregano. “I heard you all caught something,” he said. “Thought I’d help.”

Grandma Dot accepted the casserole like a championship trophy. “We did catch something, Mr. Alvarez. But we cannot throw it. We cannot punt it. We cannot set it down and tiptoe away like it’s a sleeping cat.”

Mr. Alvarez nodded sympathetically. “But you can share it.”

“Not helping,” said everyone, and then they laughed, which turned into a chorus of coughs, which turned into utter silence while they listened to the brave little casserole bubble.

They gathered around the coffee table, wrapped in blankets and wisdom. Milo scribbled a note for his school report: “Hypothesis: You can catch a cOLd, but not throw it. Data: Grandma tried to fastball one into a laundry basket. Result: Laundry basket remains un-impressed.”

For the finale, Grandma lifted her spoon like a baton and declared: *Sometimes the punchline is the cure—if not for the sniffles, then at least for the mood.*

They ate. They sniffled in harmony. And somewhere in the middle of their collective wheeze, Milo grinned. Riddle solved. Joke told. The house warmed by soup, sympathy, and the shared understanding that not everything you catch is meant to fly.

Place the seat in the back seat, away from active airbags; the center position is often safest if it allows a secure fit. Check the seat’s expiration date and ensure all parts are present and undamaged.

Get the recline angle right. For rear-facing seats, use the built-in level indicators to keep your baby’s airway open; newborns usually need a more reclined angle than older infants. Press down on the car seat base with your body weight while tightening the LATCH strap or seat belt to remove slack. The seat should not move more than 1 inch side-to-side or front-to-back at the belt path.

Harness your child correctly every ride. Position the harness at or below the shoulders for rear-facing, and at or above for forward-facing. Perform the pinch test: tighten until you can’t pinch any webbing at the collarbone. Chest clip should be at armpit level. Avoid bulky coats; use thin layers and a blanket over the harness if needed.

elm Do a professional check. Many fire stations, pediatric clinics, or certified Child Passenger Safety Technicians offer free inspections. Bring the seat, your child, and manuals. Recheck after switching vehicles, washing covers, or adjusting harness height. As your child grows, follow height and weight limits and keep rear-facing as long as allowed for maximum safety.

***
Part 2. Motivation
- Users need to quickly narrow large catalogs by attributes (brand, price, ratings, categories).
- Current search is slow and limited to exact matches; it increases bounce rates and support load.
- Advanced Search improves conversion, reduces time-to-product, and enables marketing to create targeted landing pages.

***
Part 3. Milestone objectives
- M1: Requirements and design

  - Define API contract (query params, response shape, error codes).
  - Select and justify search backend approach (Postgres + trigram/GIN vs. OpenSearch).
  - Data model and indexing strategy documented.
- M2: Backend query layer
  - Implement search service with filter parsing, validation, and query builder.
  - Support AND/OR filters, ranges, and multi-select facets.
  - Implement sort options (relevance, price asc/desc, rating desc, newest).
  - Implement pagination (cursor-based) with stable ordering.
  - Partial-match search with stemming and n-grams; basic typo tolerance.
- M3: Indexing and data pipeline
  - Create indexes (e.g., GIN/GIN_trgm for Postgres or analyzers/mappings for OpenSearch).
  - Build incremental sync from Product DB to search index with change data capture.
  - Backfill job for full reindex and monitoring for lag/failures.
- M4: Faceting and aggregations

- Gather use cases: percentage rollouts, user targeting, environment scoping, dynamic configs.

2) Control plane API
- REST endpoints: CRUD for flags, segments, environments, projects; evaluation endpoint; audit log query.

3) Admin UI
- React app with flag list, detail editor (rules, variants, rollout %), environments overview.
- Real-time status on propagation; diff view and change history.
- Guardrails: confirmation for production changes, scheduled rollouts, freeze windows.

4) SDKs and evaluation
- Server SDK (Node/TS) and Web SDK:
  - Bootstrapping from signed config.
  - Local evaluation engine (deterministic bucketing by user key; rule evaluation).
  - In-memory + persistent cache; background streaming or polling updates.
  - Offline mode and defaults; event hooks for exposure metrics.
- Stateless evaluation API for non-SDK clients; edge cache via CDN.

5) Distribution and propagation
- Config store: PostgreSQL for control, Redis for hot config, object store for signed config blobs.
- Pub/sub: Redis Streams or NATS to notify SDK gateways; long-poll/Server-Sent Events.
- Edge caching: CDN cache of signed configs per environment with short TTL + ETag.

6) Observability and governance
- Audit logging for all mutations with actor, before/after, reason.
- Metrics: request rate/latency, cache hit ratio, update lag, SDK error rates.
- Alerts: stale cache, failed propagations, high 5xx, unusual change surges.
- Compliance: data retention policy; PII minimization (hashed user keys).

7) Testing and reliability
- Unit tests for rule engine and bucketing determinism.
- Contract tests from OpenAPI; SDK compatibility matrix.
- Chaos tests: message bus delay, cache eviction, partial outages.
- Load test: 10k RPS evals, 1k flags, 1M users; failover drills.

- Sign configs (Ed25519) and verify in SDKs; rotate keys.
- TLS everywhere; CSP for UI; secure headers.
- Least-privilege DB roles; secret management via vault.
- Rate limiting/token scoping; audit for admin actions.

9) Deployment and ops
- Infra as code (Terraform): API, UI, Redis, Postgres HA, message bus, CDN.
- Blue/green deploys; database migrations with zero-downtime strategy.
- Runbooks: incident response, rollback, key rotation, SDK deprecation.

- Quickstart guides; SDK API docs; migration guide from env vars/toggles.
- Examples: percentage rollout, targeted cohort, kill switch, staged rollout.
- Internal training session and office hours.

He checked his mail at half-past three, beside the ficus tree,
A scroll with crimson wax appeared—addressed “To Noble He.”
An emissary, plumed and prim, with trumpet made of tin,
Proclaimed, “Good sir, the king of Ngária declares you next of kin!”

The neighbors peered o’er picket fence; the cat looked on askance;
His slippers quaked; his teacup shook; his bathrobe tried to dance.
“Your highness-cousin!” cried the herald, “Pack thy socks and ring—
For fate hath spun a wondrous web: you’re kin to Nigeria’s king!”

He bowed as though he meant it, though his knees said otherwise,
He Googled “how to monarch” while he polished alibis.
A crown? Perhaps. A throne? Why not! A yacht? He’d settle, sure—
But first he asked, “Does cousinhood come with dental and a chauffeur?”

The emissary flourished scrolls, with seals like candied plums,
A family tree that branched so wide it needed extra thumbs.
“Our records show,” the herald sang, “your granddad’s brother’s niece
Once shared a mango with a prince—behold! Dynastic peace!”

He tried the royal wave and poked himself twice in the eye,
He practiced signing napkins with a flourish 10 feet high.
His dog became Lord Biscuit; the goldfish, Duchess Gill;
He knighted the zucchini and the neighbor’s daffodil.

“But tell me,” said our hero, as his robe dragged down the stair,
“If I’m so very royal, do I still need bus fare?”
“Fear not,” the envoy nodded, “for we’ll sort the petty things;
However, there’s a processing fee, and twenty thousand rings.”

He paused, and then he chuckled, and he checked the wax again—
A smudge that read “Sincerely, A. Scamuel, Your Best Friend.”
He bowed right back, shut tight the door, and brewed a knowing tea—
Proclaiming to the cat, “Henceforth, I’m Duke of Skepticy.”

And yet at night he dreamed of drums and palm-frond shaded springs,
Of cousins thrice-removed who taught the parrots how to sing—
He woke and pinned a sticky note upon his humble wall:
*“Beware of sudden royalty—unless they text, not call.”*
